directAnswer: Pope Clement VII was Giulio de' Medici, cousin of Leo X, who reigned from 1523 to 1534. His pontificate saw the Sack of Rome by imperial troops in 1527, his refusal to annul the marriage of Henry VIII and Catherine of Aragon, the coronation of Charles V at Bologna, and the approval of the Capuchin friars.

sections.h2: Giulio de' Medici, Cousin of Leo X
paras: Giulio de' Medici was born in Florence in 1478, the son of Giuliano de' Medici, who was killed in the Pazzi conspiracy a month before his birth. He was raised in the household of his uncle Lorenzo the Magnificent alongside his cousin Giovanni.

When Giovanni became Leo X, he made Giulio archbishop of Florence and a cardinal in 1513, and Giulio became his chief adviser. After the short reign of Adrian VI, Giulio was elected on 19 November 1523 and took the name Clement VII.

sections.h2: Between Emperor and King: The Sack of Rome
paras: Clement VII inherited a papacy caught in the rivalry between Emperor Charles V and King Francis I of France. His shifting alliances, culminating in the League of Cognac with France in 1526, angered the emperor.

In May 1527 unpaid imperial troops, many of them German mercenaries, stormed Rome and sacked it for weeks. Most of the Swiss Guard died on 6 May defending the pope's escape to Castel Sant'Angelo, a sacrifice still commemorated each year when new guards are sworn in. Clement was held for months before escaping to Orvieto. He later reconciled with Charles and crowned him emperor at Bologna in February 1530, the last papal coronation of an emperor.

Henry VIII sought an annulment of his marriage to Catherine of Aragon, the aunt of Charles V. Clement delayed for years, sending Cardinal Campeggio to hear the case in England in 1529 before recalling it to Rome.

After Henry married Anne Boleyn in 1533, Clement declared the action invalid and threatened excommunication, and in March 1534 he ruled that Henry's marriage to Catherine was valid. Within months Parliament passed the Act of Supremacy, separating the Church of England from Rome.

sections.h2: Capuchins, Theatines, and the Last Judgment
paras: Clement VII approved the Theatines in 1524 and the Capuchin reform of the Franciscans in 1528, both important in the Catholic renewal that followed. In 1533 he arranged the marriage of his young relative Catherine de' Medici to the future Henry II of France.

A patron of Michelangelo, he oversaw work on the Medici Chapel in Florence and asked the artist to paint the Last Judgment on the Sistine altar wall, a work carried out under his successor. That same year he heard an explanation of Copernicus's ideas about the sun-centered universe in the Vatican gardens. Clement VII died on 25 September 1534.

keyFacts: Born Giulio de' Medici in Florence in 1478; cousin of Leo X
Sack of Rome by imperial troops in May 1527
Crowned Charles V emperor at Bologna in 1530
Refused Henry VIII's annulment; upheld his marriage to Catherine in 1534

faqs.question: What happened to Clement VII during the Sack of Rome?
faqs.answer: As imperial troops entered Rome on 6 May 1527, he fled to Castel Sant'Angelo while the Swiss Guard fought a rearguard action. He remained a virtual prisoner for months before escaping to Orvieto.

faqs.question: Why did Clement VII refuse Henry VIII's annulment?
faqs.answer: He was not persuaded the marriage to Catherine of Aragon was invalid, and political pressure from her nephew Charles V weighed heavily. In 1534 he formally declared the marriage valid.

faqs.question: Did Clement VII commission the Last Judgment?
faqs.answer: He asked Michelangelo to paint it on the Sistine altar wall shortly before his death; the work was carried out under Paul III and finished in 1541.
